Finally, the panel discussed offering benefits to councillors, in the hopes of encouraging parents and younger people to run. When staff asked for a quote for councillor benefits in 2023, they received a quote for $462 per person per month, or $27,720 per year. The panel opted instead to recommend a $1000 per year health spending account for each councillor. The panel recommended increasing the mayor’s remuneration by 10 per cent, bringing the total to about $25,500 before being adjusted for inflation. Likewise, the panel recommended a 10 per cent increase to councillors’ remuneration, raising it to about $13,100 before being adjusted for inflation. It also recommended giving individual travel budgets to each elected official, with $7,000 per councillor and $14,000 for the mayor, totalling $42K. Valemount’s remuneration reviews take place every four years, prior to municipal elections. Yanciw said Council’s decision would be impacting future councillors, though Council could choose to implement the recommendations in 2026. “You are not doing this for yourselves. We have an election less than a year from now, and there will be a new council to whom this will apply,” she said. Torgerson thanked Yanciw for her presentation and Council received the delegation for information. ## Transportation planning grant Council approved staff to apply to the UBCM Active Transportation Planning Grant, which supports local governments to incorporate transportation planning into formal documents, such as the Official Community Plan. Staff will apply to the grant to create a transportation master plan, which will allow the Village to see how infrastructure can be improved to promote more active transportation, such as walking and cycling. It also includes a new policy that says the Village will support the development of affordable housing by permitting a wide variety of housing types, working with non-profits, and investigating reductions to minimum parking requirements. ## Fees and Charges bylaw Council gave third reading to a fees and charges amendment bylaw which increases fees to allow the Village to save more revenue which will be spent on maintaining assets in the future. Increased fees include residential water use, which is increasing from $487.40 to $519.31; residential sewer rates, increasing from $601.46 to $646.57; and commercial water use, increasing from $600.24 to $639.26, among others. ## Remuneration bylaw Council gave first and second reading to the updated Council Remuneration Bylaw. Following the remuneration panel’s recommendations, the updated bylaw increases remuneration for the mayor by about $2,300 and for each councillor by about $1,200, along with an annual increase for inflation based on the BC Consumer Price Index. The recommendation also includes providing each elected official with a $1,000 per year health spending account. ## Event Attendance Policy Council approved an event attendance policy based on the remuneration review panel’s recommendations. Currently, councillors draw from a pooled fund to pay for event attendance. The panel recommended providing $7,000 in travel spending to each councillor and $14,000 to the mayor each year. ## Adjournment Mayor Owen Torgerson adjourned the meeting at 8:49 p.m.

Abigail Popple May 21, 2026 ## McBride Council: mini soccer field, 2026 budget, water source By Abigail Popple, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter McBride Council discussed a potential soccer field, the 2026 budget and pursuing a new water source during its regular April 28th meeting. Mayor Gene Runtz called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. Council amended the agenda to add three late items: minutes from the April 14th regular meeting, a monthly update from the Public Works Department, and written comments from residents about the 2026-2030 Five Year Financial Plan. Council adopted the minutes from the April 14th meeting and moved on to hear a delegation about building a miniature soccer field.  ### Soccer field  Local youth sports organizer Meagan Ryan gave a presentation requesting support in principle for a grant that would fund a miniature soccer field. ### Financial plan comments Resident Rick Thompson sent 10 questions to the Village regarding the 2026-2030 Five Year Financial Plan. First, Thompson noted that the Village is projecting about $20K less in tax revenue for 2026 than it received in 2025. He added that the Village had projected about $691K in tax revenue in the 2025 budget, but at the end of the year had received $682K. He asked why there was a disparity between the projected 2026 revenue and the 2025 actual revenue. Financial consultant Karen Stahl said the Village has decided to change how “payments in lieu of taxes,” or PILs, are reflected in the budget. A payment in lieu is used when a government keeps property in the jurisdiction of another government – for example, the Regional District uses some property within the boundaries of the Village of McBride. A government cannot tax another government, so McBride collects payments from the property users and sends a portion of the payments to the Regional District.  Stahl said payments in lieu of taxes used to be included in the budget, but since a portion of those payments flow up to the Regional District, the Village decided not to include them in this year’s net tax revenue. Thompson had two questions about service fee revenue, which is partly made up of business license fees. In 2025, the Village received nearly $17K in service fee revenue, while the projected revenue in 2026 is about $11K. He asked if the Village is issuing fewer business licenses this year, and if there were other reasons for a lower projected revenue this year. Stahl said last year’s revenue was higher because the Village received money for hosting the agriculture forum last fall, and a similar event has not been confirmed for this year. She added that the $11K is still just a project and this year’s actual service fee revenue may be higher. Thompson said this year’s projected grant revenue of $8.3M is over twice as high as last year’s $2.9M, and asked for a breakdown of how grant funding this year will be allocated. Stahl said the Village is hoping for a $3.3M grant from the Canada Community Building Fund for sewer infrastructure improvements, and that money is included in the projected grant revenue. Additionally, the Village already received $1.3M to install universal water meters this year, a $2.6M grant from UBCM for water filtration improvements, and $500K for improving lighting along the airport runway. Miscellaneous smaller grants bring the number up to around $8.3M, she said. Thompson also asked about the budget for general common services, which are the payments the Village makes on staff salaries, Council remuneration and property insurance. During the April 14th meeting, Stahl had projected this expenditure at $1,196,522, compared to the 2025 expenditure of $1,013,475, which Thompson noted was an 18 per cent increase. Stahl said she has revised her calculations since the April 14th meeting, and found that the 2025 expenditure was actually $1,106,000, and the 2026 projection has been lowered to $1,122,000. Thompson noted that last year, the expenditures for protective services – which include payment for bylaw officers and emergency management expenses – came out to just about $4K, though the Village had projected $18K. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Valemount | McBride | Dunster | Blue River (https://www.therockymountaingoat.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/JAN-23-RMG-MASTER-FINAL_compressed.pdf) 【turn741921search13】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 1.8 years ago; Crawled: 1.8 years ago; Valemount | McBride | Dunster | Blue River ... ## Comparison communities for Council remuneration ...
